1621: The most weakly attested NT book in the early centuries. Origen notes doubts about it; Eusebius lists it among the antilegomena and says it was not received as canonical by many, though useful (Church History 3.3, 3.25). Jerome reports that many doubted it because its style differs from 1 Peter. It is absent from the Muratorian fragment and the Syriac Peshitta, but it appears in P72 (third/fourth century), was accepted by Athanasius (367) and the African councils, and has been in every major canon since.
1624: The apostle John, author of the Fourth Gospel, writing as an elderly eyewitness in Ephesus.
1625: Anonymous in the text. Most scholars attribute it to the same circle (and often the same author) as the Gospel of John, with debate over whether the writer was the apostle, John the Elder or another leader of the Johannine community. It claims eyewitness contact with the 'word of life' (1 John 1:1-3).
1626: Shortly after the Gospel of John
1627: Earlier (before 70) on early dating of John
1628: Johannine churches, likely in and around Ephesus, shaken by a schism.
1629: A group had left the community (1 John 2:19), apparently denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh and claiming sinlessness while neglecting love.
1630: To give assurance of eternal life to those who believe, and to supply tests of true faith: right belief about Jesus, obedience and love.
1631: God is light and God is love
1633: Jesus Christ come in the flesh
1635: Walking in the light and confessing sin
1636: Prologue: the word of life we have seen and touched
1637: Walking in the light: sin, confession, obedience
1638: Antichrists and abiding in the truth
1639: Children of God: righteousness and love
1640: Test the spirits; God is love
1641: Faith that overcomes; assurance of life
1642: Written to a church wounded by people leaving, 1 John tells those who stayed how they can know they have eternal life: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, they keep his commands, and they love one another, because God is love.
1643: Among the recognised books (homologoumena) from the second century; used by Polycarp and Papias according to Eusebius. The 'Johannine Comma' (the Trinitarian addition in 1 John 5:7-8 in the KJV) is absent from early Greek manuscripts and is regarded as a later Latin addition by most scholars.
1646: The apostle John, styling himself 'the elder'.
1647: Written by 'the elder' (2 John 1:1), whom many scholars distinguish from the apostle, sometimes identifying him with John the Elder mentioned by Papias; others hold the elder is the apostle. Same author as 3 John and closely related to 1 John.
1649: 'The elect lady and her children', most likely a personified local church.
1650: Travelling teachers denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh were seeking hospitality from congregations.
1651: To urge love and obedience and to warn the church not to welcome or support deceivers who deny the incarnation.
1653: The incarnation as a test of truth
1657: Beware of deceivers; do not receive them
1659: In the shortest book of the New Testament the elder reminds a church of the old command to love one another, and warns it not to give a platform to teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.
1660: Antilegomena. Irenaeus quotes it, and the Muratorian fragment mentions two letters of John, which may be 1 and 2 John. Eusebius lists 2-3 John among the disputed books, and Origen notes that not all accepted them. Both are absent from the Syriac Peshitta, but they were received by Athanasius and the African councils.
1663: The same 'elder' as 2 John; identity debated as for 2 John (the apostle or John the Elder).
1664: Gaius, a faithful believer known for hospitality.
1665: Diotrephes, who loved to be first, was refusing to receive the elder's messengers and expelling those who did.
1666: To commend Gaius for supporting travelling missionaries, rebuke Diotrephes, and recommend Demetrius.
1670: Gaius commended for walking in truth
1673: This brief note shows early church life at ground level: travelling teachers depending on hospitality, a generous host, and a local leader who shuts the door on them. The elder urges Gaius to imitate what is good.
1674: Antilegomena, with the weakest early attestation of the Johannine letters; Eusebius lists it as disputed and it is absent from the Syriac Peshitta. It was received by Athanasius (367) and the councils of Hippo and Carthage.
1677: Jude (Judas), brother of James and so a brother of Jesus (Jude 1:1).
1678: Divided. Some scholars see it as pseudonymous, citing its competent Greek and references to 'the faith once delivered' as signs of a later period. Others think a brother of Jesus is a plausible author, noting that a forger would more likely choose a more prominent name, and that its Jewish apocalyptic world fits early Palestinian Christianity.
1681: An unnamed community, probably of Jewish Christians familiar with Jewish traditions such as 1 Enoch.
1682: Intruders had slipped into the church, turning grace into licence and rejecting authority.
1683: To urge readers to contend for the faith, to expose the intruders through Old Testament and Jewish examples of judgment, and to keep believers in God's love.
1687: God's power to keep from stumbling
1689: Examples of judgment: Israel, angels, Sodom
1690: The intruders described; Michael, Cain, Balaam, Korah, Enoch
1693: Jude meant to write about salvation but instead had to sound an alarm about people corrupting grace. He piles up examples of judgment from Israel's history and tradition, then closes with one of Scripture's best-loved doxologies to the God who keeps his people from falling.
1694: Antilegomena. It is listed in the Muratorian fragment and used by Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria, but Jerome reports that many rejected it because it cites 1 Enoch (Jude 1:14-15) and alludes to the Assumption of Moses (Jude 1:9). Eusebius lists it as disputed and it is absent from the Syriac Peshitta. It was received by Athanasius and the African councils.
1697: John the apostle, exiled on Patmos (Rev 1:9); Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 81) and Irenaeus name the apostle.
1698: The author calls himself John, a servant and prophet, but not an apostle. Dionysius of Alexandria (third century, quoted in Eusebius, Church History 7.25) already argued from its very different Greek style that it was not by the author of the Gospel. Most modern scholars think it was written by a Christian prophet named John, distinct from the apostle; a minority still defends apostolic authorship.
1699: Domitianic dating, following Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3); majority view
1700: Neronian dating, before the fall of Jerusalem (preterist and some critical scholars)
1701: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea.
1702: Churches under pressure from emperor worship and civic religion, local hostility and the temptations of compromise and wealth, whether under Nero or Domitian.
1703: To reveal the true state of things behind the visible world: Christ reigns, evil will be judged, and the faithful will share in his victory. It calls the churches to repent, endure and refuse compromise with idolatrous power.
1704: Christ the slain Lamb who reigns
1706: Faithful witness and endurance through suffering
1707: Judgment on Babylon and the beast
1709: New heaven, new earth and new Jerusalem
1712: Heavenly throne room and the Lamb with the scroll
1716: The dragon, the beasts and the Lamb's followers
1717: Seven bowls and the fall of Babylon
1720: The thousand years and final judgment
1721: New heaven, new earth, new Jerusalem
1723: Revelation pulls back the curtain on a world where Rome looked all-powerful, showing a throne in heaven and a slain Lamb who holds history's scroll. Through vivid symbolic visions it calls the churches to faithful witness, and it ends where Genesis began, with God dwelling among his people in a renewed creation.
1724: The canonical history of Revelation runs opposite to that of Hebrews. It was accepted early in the West (Justin, Irenaeus, the Muratorian fragment) but became doubted in the East after Dionysius of Alexandria questioned its apostolic authorship. Eusebius wavered, placing it among the recognised books 'if it seem proper' and also among the spurious. It is missing from the list attributed to the Synod of Laodicea (canon 60, authenticity debated), from Cyril of Jerusalem's list, and from the Syriac Peshitta. Athanasius included it in 367, and the West never doubted it; it is still not read in the Eastern Orthodox lectionary. Luther (1522) said he could not detect the Holy Spirit in it, and Zwingli did not regard it as a book of the Bible, yet both left it in their Bibles.
